conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re here because of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve had this pain in my belly for a couple days. I’ve thrown up twice. And swallowing hurts—like something’s stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned chest discomfort and shortness of breath too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I think that’s from the pain. It hurts so much when I try to eat or drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of radiation for tracheal cancer, we’re concerned about inflammation or narrowing in your esophagus. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before—radiation esophagitis. But this feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check for infection too. Being on steroids increases your risk for a yeast infection in the esophagus, called candidiasis. We’re starting fluconazole just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve taken that before. But what about the pain? I can’t even keep water down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran for nausea and will keep you hydrated with IV fluids. We also have a mouthwash with lidocaine and Maalox to numb the pain when you swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That sounds helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. White count is normal, so no sign of bacterial infection. Your sputum test was also normal—just typical mouth bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the flu test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Negative. So it’s not influenza. Your cough and congestion are likely from a mild viral upper respiratory infection, which should improve on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what about the swallowing issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a barium swallow today to look for any narrowing in your esophagus. Given your history, we’re worried about a stricture from past radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The barium swallow shows a narrowing in your esophagus, about 3 cm long, right at the level of your aortic arch. A 12-mm tablet couldn’t pass through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean I can’t eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But we’re not going to dilate it today because there’s too much inflammation. We’ll reduce the swelling first. We’ll do an endoscopy soon to look more closely and take biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve increased your prednisone to 40 mg daily for a week to help with your arthritis pain, then taper down. I know you felt worse when you were off it last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain was terrible. Thank you for restarting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also switching your Nexium to pantoprazole twice a day. It’s stronger and will help reduce stomach acid, which may be irritating your esophagus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’m still on the fluconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for 14 days. We’re treating for possible candida, especially since you’re on steroids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea has improved, and you’re tolerating liquids. Your abdominal pain is much better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had some broth this morning. Felt okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll advance you to soft foods. Your bowel regimen is helping too—no constipation now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the endoscopy this morning. There’s severe inflammation and an ulcer at 20 cm in your esophagus. We also saw a small nodule and took biopsies from both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An ulcer? Is it from the radiation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. The biopsies will tell us more—whether it’s just inflammation or something else. We couldn’t dilate the stricture today because it was too inflamed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can we try dilation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In a few months, once the inflammation settles. Your GI doctor will schedule a follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nodule? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small, and we don’t think it’s cancerous, but the biopsy will confirm. Most likely it’s scar tissue from radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid. The old scarring from radiation is still there, but nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My cough is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your oxygen levels are normal. We’ll keep you on your asthma meds—Advair, Spiriva, and nebulizers as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high. We’re keeping you on your usual meds—amlodipine, lisinopril, and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It runs high when I’m in pain. Is it better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s coming down. We gave you a dose of Lasix yesterday because we saw some leg swelling—just a little fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that at home when my feet swell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll send you home with it to use as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. You’re eating, pain is controlled, and your breathing is stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the fluconazole for 14 days. Take pantoprazole twice daily. And follow the prednisone taper: start at 20 mg, then reduce by 2.5 mg each week until you’re at 5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and stop ranitidine—you don’t need it with pantoprazole. Also stop cetirizine; it may be making you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. I thought it was the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly that, but cetirizine can add to it. We’re also stopping metoclopramide since your nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a call from GI in about a week with the results. Please follow up with them and your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll arrange home health to help you for a few days. Keep using the lidocaine-Maalox mix for pain before meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Especially if pain returns, or you can’t keep food down. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mrs. ___. We’re glad you’re feeling better.
